en: Search every one of their bundles.
Act according to their bloodline;
Slaughter all their people without leaving one.
Violate their beautiful women,
Scatter their honor like ashes.
Press the attack fiercely;
Take revenge for that ancient grudge!
They speak their own stammering tongue,
And harbor hatred toward us.
Their heads are black and their feet are cloven;
Treat those wretches like cattle,
Humiliate them and make them slaves.
Slaughter every last hero
Who might strike back.
Plan well and start the conflict;
Rip open their pregnant women.
Burn them until no smoke remains,
Slaughter them and leave no descendants.
Gouge out the eyes with spears
Of the heroes who stand against you!
Find a way to settle their account;
Strike down the ancient devil's great rage
Until he loses his senses!
Separate out their strongest men;
Inspect their treasury and goods.
Bundles, saddlebags, and packs—
Take all these as plunder;
Bring ruin upon them in this way.
If there is a hero or lion among them,
If there is a man who boasts of strength,
Come out and face him in single combat!
Thus spoke Chyntengir,
And issued a harsh command.
Such was the khan's command.
Onto the vast field of battle,
To the place where they would clash,
Odukan came out for single combat—
A descendant of the Black Kalmyks,
An heir of mighty Joloy.
His strength was extraordinary;
He traveled on foot without mounting a horse—
Who had ever known such a giant!
Do not ask what Odukan was like:
His eyes were those of a black demon,
He was the very embodiment of calamity.
His head was like a cauldron
On the body of a dying boar;
His brows were like a dog lying in wait.
When he attacked, he swept men away;
When giants charged, he destroyed them.
Once a one-eyed giant came,
A khan who knew no peace.
They fought savagely,
Standing against each other in battle.
He drank and was never sated with blood;
When he struck, he spared no life.
He blunted blades of steel,
And destroyed invincible giants.
He grew up in the desert, reeking of poison,
And on the cliffs, reeking of blood.
He roamed about cutting off heads,
Killing men and laying waste to peoples;
He had shaken many lands.
He was himself a bloodthirsty scourge.
At the sight of him Kakan and Chyn,
And at his valor Bakburchun,
Uluntu and Dynsha lost heart.
His strength and courage
Were renowned throughout these lands.
When he faced a man, he spared no life;
Even half a boar's carcass
Would not half-fill his belly.
He gathered his courage and prepared;
Inspiration came to him from the unseen.
When his khan gave the command,
Would Odu merely stand and watch?
Would God strike Odu down?
He mounted mountain-like Kongkul,
Divided Kongkul's tail in twelve,
And tied each part in a sharp knot.
He girded himself in mountain-like iron.
Hanging at his arm
Was an iron mace as large as a yurt:
If you take fright, flee far away;
If you meet it in fury,
Your poor head will be smashed to pieces.
He lashed the horse Kongkul,
And thundered out his challenge:
“Let not merely one of you, but a thousand
Heroes of the Burut people charge me!
If you would fight, the Kakan host is ready;
I, blood-drinking Odu, am ready!
All of you, come here!” he cried.
He came onto the battlefield shouting,
Making heaven and earth resound:
“Leave your weaklings; send your lions!
Send the bravest of your heroes!
Beneath me is my horse Kongkul;
Today I have the strength
To destroy the whole wide world!”
Thus he thundered,
Standing there in fury.
Wondering what horror this might be,
The people trembled.
As the people stood so,
Er Kogoy, father of the nation,
Whose mount was Toburchak,
Leapt down from his steed
And turned his face toward the qibla.
Before Kenen, pillar of the people,
He now asked for a blessing:
“Black-maned leopard,
Descendant of the lion hero,
Your first ancestor was Tugol Khan,
Blessed by Khydyr from the beginning.
All your forefathers were khans;
The forty saints aided them of old.
Each time one died, his line flourished;
Khidyr himself followed him.
Your ancestors planted banners on grassy lands
And brought fire upon
Those who came in arrogance!
Heed what your elder,
The hero Kogoy, says;
Grant me your highest blessing!
If death comes and my days end,
If I perish from a stray shot,
And am destroyed by a chance blow,
Say that renowned Kogoy died,
That this honored, precious soul
Gave the life that was needed
For the soaring Ala-Too,
For the white-capped Kyrgyz people,
For honor and for dignity;
Bury me with your own hands!
To go against Odukan,
And answer the infidel who humiliates us,
If death does not take me—
Noble white-capped Kyrgyz people,
With Er Kenen in your midst…”
Every wise diviner,
Every hero from whom wisdom springs,
Spread their palms and gave their hands.
They gave him armor no bullet could pierce,
A helmet of blue steel,
And richly fashioned plate armor.
They dressed him in blue steel
Beautifully suited to his body.
Toburchak, with his handsome neck,
Who grazed on the Chambyl ridge,
Born a true racing steed,
They gave Er Kogoy to mount.
They clasped and pressed his hand,
Entrusted him to the spirits of the ancestors
And to the Creator,
And sent Kogoy forth.
Toward fork-necked Akyska,
Toward remote Tankyska,
Into mist beyond the reach of sight,
To the very edge of the haze,
To the yellow plain where battle was joined,
Across the face of that yellow plain,
Kogoy rode.
When Odukan saw him,
His eyes flashed like a lion's.
A fit of rage seized him;
He ground and gnashed
Those gate-like front teeth.
He turned his rhinoceros mouth,
Cut a road across the plain,
And attacked Er Kogoy.
The hero on one side and giant on the other
Shouted and leveled their spears;
They fought by turns.
They measured and matched each other,
Fighting with spears.
They came at one another head-on
And fought with iron maces.
The rim of the blue-steel helmet
Was battered and crushed.
The broad-rumped bay stallion with mattock-like hooves,
Who never tired on patrol,
Toburchak of the open steppe,
Had his back broken.
His wings were clipped—
What could our elder Kogoy do?
He was parted from Toburchak.
A bullet brought Toburchak down,
And the foe tore Kogoy's coat.
Then Er Kogoy
Bent at the waist from fighting on foot.
His frail life was pressed hard;
His strength failed and calamity came.
It became a night that blinded the eyes,
A day of disaster to behold.
Not letting his wound-up turban fall,
Not letting Er Odu take him,
He fought beyond all measure—
Who had ever seen such a deed!
Blood flowed from his dark eyes;
Poor Kogoy was bewildered.
His two hands that had served him
Could no longer rise and were paralyzed.
His precious head, the lock of life,
Became a red bucket of blood.
He lost consciousness and bled,
His strength gone, his body weak.
His dear eyes seemed about to close,
Drooping and hanging dimly.
Accursed pale Death
Was seen approaching his brow.
Odukan stood there thus.
A prince among his Kaldays,
A cruel prince who had seen much,
A slave-marksman who never missed,
Proud of his marksmanship,
Hid behind him.
“Aim between the forked shoulders;
The face of the skull is the mark,
The very center of the measure.”
He set a bullet as large as a sheep's head
Firmly against the sight,
Bound it to certain death,
And struck, splitting his head.
His soul left before the smoke cleared;
The fatal bullet struck his temple.
Our poor elder Kogoy
Had departed for Mecca.
Seeing this, Ebegey cried:
“Rather than lose my comrade
And let the Kyrgyz be cast into fire,
Rather than lose one of my horns
And remain a hornless beast,
Rather than lose mane and tail
And remain a stunted thing,
May I sink unborn into the deep;
May I die and not remain alive!
My figure before me,
My watchful Kogoy,
My bannered mountain ridge
No enemy caravan could cross,
My greatest lion in time of need—
Let me die for my twin!
My truly created golden soul,
If the Creator truly wills it,
I will give up this fly-like life.”
Thus Ebegey spoke,
Whipping the gray racer Aksutkul
From side to side,
Driving him right and left.
He struck the stallion's flank
And shouted, “Comrade!”
As he attacked Er Odu.
They stood face-to-face,
Loosened the mouths of their steeds,
And without frowning or knitting a brow,
